Her cultural reach has also shown up in unexpected places. Wyclef Jean once recorded a song inspired by her, a marker of how far Williams had traveled beyond sports pages and tournament broadcasts. She became not only a tennis star, but a pop-cultural figure — someone whose name could stand for strength, elegance, ambition and Black excellence.

Yet Williams has often spoken about fame with caution. Celebrity, in her telling, is not the point; work is. Faith has also been central to her life, shaping how she discusses pressure, success and setbacks. Raised as a Jehovah’s Witness, she has credited her beliefs with helping her keep perspective in a career defined by scrutiny.

And tennis, despite everything else, remains the axis. The businesses, photo shoots and public attention may surround her, but the court is where the world first learned how to read Venus Williams: as a competitor who changed the speed of the women’s game, challenged institutions, fought for equal prize money and carried herself like someone who knew her worth before everyone else caught up.

The familiar image endures — Venus on court, ready to serve — but it is only one portrait among many.
